title: Data Centers in Orbit: Why Big Tech Wants to Move AI's Power Problem to Space
author: Kenji Nakamoto

sources_used.note: No other cached research/*.json files were topically relevant to orbital compute/data-center power infrastructure (existing cache is medicine, robotics IPOs, data-broker privacy, AI regulation/DOJ, hallucination/misinformation, and prompt economics articles) — went straight to WebSearch/WebFetch per priority order, since the curated RSS list (NASA, ESA, Space.com, etc.) requires live feed pulls not available as static fetches in this pass; findings below are cross-checked across Google's own primary source, trade press (DCD, GeekWire, TechCrunch, Fortune), and independent technical/skeptic analysis (IEEE Spectrum, SpaceNews/Varda).

statistics.stat: Worldwide data center power demand is projected to rise 27% in 2026 to reach 132 gigawatts (GW), up from 104GW in 2025, and is estimated to hit 290GW by 2030. Global data center electricity consumption is projected to grow 26% in 2026 to 565 terawatt-hours (TWh), exceeding 1,200 TWh by 2030.

AI-optimized servers alone consumed roughly 95 TWh globally in 2025 and are projected to draw 175 TWh in 2026 (an 84% jump), reaching 258 TWh in 2027 — the first year AI hardware is expected to consume more electricity than all conventional (non-AI) data center servers combined. Data centers are adding 5-7 GW of new load annually while new grid generation capacity comes online at only 2-3 GW/year, a gap expected to persist through 2032.

Google's Project Suncatcher research (published November 4, 2025) finds solar panels in the right orbit can achieve up to 8x the productivity of Earth-based solar installations, with near-continuous illumination in a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit (~650km altitude). Google's illustrative design uses an 81-satellite constellation flown in a ~1km-radius cluster, 100-200m apart, linked by free-space optical inter-satellite links (bench-demonstrated at 800 Gbps each-way per transceiver pair) carrying Trillium (v6e) Cloud TPUs. Radiation testing found TPU high-bandwidth memory showed irregularities only after 2 krad(Si) of exposure — nearly 3x the anticipated five-year mission dose of 750 rad(Si). Google projects launch costs could fall under $200/kg by the mid-2030s, the point at which it estimates space-based data center operating costs become comparable to terrestrial facilities on a per-kilowatt/year basis.

Starcloud (Redmond, WA) raised a $170M Series A led by Benchmark and EQT Ventures, hitting a $1.1B valuation just 17 months after its Y Combinator demo day — the fastest company in YC history to reach unicorn status. It has raised $200M total. In November 2025 it launched Starcloud-1, a 130-pound satellite carrying an Nvidia H100 chip, with Starcloud-2 (100x the power generation of Starcloud-1, carrying an Nvidia Blackwell B200) planned to follow in 2026, launched via SpaceX.

Thermal-engineering analysis of orbital GPU deployment: a single 700-watt Nvidia H100 chip needs just under 3 square meters of radiator area to hold 20°C (about 1 square meter if run hotter, at 85°C); a full 32-GPU, ~40kW AI server rack needs roughly 80 square meters of radiator — about the size of a pickleball court. Because radiative cooling follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law (radiator area scales with power and inversely with temperature to the 4th power), and because solar collection (~400 W/m²) and heat rejection (~450 W/m²) need almost the same surface area, every square meter that generates power in orbit demands roughly another square meter just to shed the heat. Radiator area needed also grows ~40% over a 5-year LEO lifespan as UV and atomic oxygen degrade radiator emissivity.

A public techno-economic model built by a Varda Space Industries engineer puts orbital compute at roughly 3x the cost per watt of terrestrial data centers in the base case — driven by launch costs, radiation-hardened hardware, and the added mass of onboard cooling and power systems (rather than tapping a shared grid).
statistics.source: Andrew McCalip (Varda Space Industries), via SpaceNews reporting

strongest_counterargument.argument: The economics remain unproven and arguably unfavorable today. Independent techno-economic modeling (Varda Space's Andrew McCalip) puts orbital compute at roughly 3x the cost per watt of terrestrial equivalents in the base case, and ABI Research's Andrew Cavalier argues the all-in cost to launch and run a single GPU in space for a year is 'at least an order of magnitude higher' than the terrestrial equivalent. The core problem is thermal, not just financial: radiative cooling in vacuum has no atmosphere or water to carry heat away, so radiator area must scale directly with power draw (a single 700W H100 needs ~3m² of radiator; a 40kW rack needs ~80m² — about a pickleball court's worth of surface area that must itself be launched, deployed, and kept working). That radiator area also degrades roughly 40% over 5 years from UV and atomic-oxygen exposure, compounding cost over the asset's life. Radiation-hardening, launch mass penalties, and space debris risk add further cost and reliability burdens with no shared power grid or on-site repair crew as a backstop. Google's own published economics concede the model only closes if launch costs fall under $200/kg (roughly 7-8x cheaper than today's ~$1,500/kg) by the mid-2030s — meaning the entire business case is a bet on future launch-cost deflation that has not yet happened, not a demonstrated advantage today.
strongest_counterargument.source: Varda Space Industries (Andrew McCalip) / ABI Research (Andrew Cavalier) / IEEE Spectrum

recent_news.item: Starcloud raises $170M Series A led by Benchmark and EQT Ventures at a $1.1B valuation — the fastest YC-backed company on record to reach unicorn status — with plans to launch Starcloud-2 (carrying an Nvidia Blackwell B200 chip, 100x the power generation of Starcloud-1) later in 2026.

February 2026 marked, per industry trade coverage, the first month in which multiple orbital data-center operators (Starcloud and others) simultaneously ran production workloads in space; separately, Starcloud filed a second FCC application proposing an 88,000-satellite processing constellation, while SpaceX/xAI (following their merger into a combined ~$1.25 trillion entity) filed for up to one million data-center satellites, and Blue Origin announced its ~5,400-satellite 'TeraWave' constellation for data-center and enterprise connectivity.

unverified_or_flagged_claims: The 'Starcloud trained an LLM and ran a version of Google Gemini in space' claim appears in secondary aggregator coverage (search-summary level) but was not independently confirmed against a primary Starcloud or Google statement in this pass — attribute cautiously if used, or omit.

SpaceX/xAI's filing for 'up to one million' data-center satellites and Starcloud's 88,000-satellite filing are both FCC filings, not built or operational constellations — these are regulatory/paperwork milestones, not deployed capacity; do not imply the satellites exist or are launching on a firm schedule.

The $5,000-per-delivered-watt 'competitive with terrestrial hyperscale' estimate (from an independent analyst calculator, andrewmccalip.com) is a modeled/contested figure, not a company-disclosed cost — it also conflicts directionally with the same source's separate 3x-cost-per-watt headline finding depending on assumptions used (launch cost, lifetime, financing); present as one contested model output, not a settled number.

Direct DataCenterDynamics fetch for Project Suncatcher (datacenterdynamics.com) returned HTTP 403 in this research pass — all Suncatcher technical figures here are sourced instead directly from Google Research's own primary blog post, which is the stronger source anyway.

Pichai's quote is from a December 2025 interview, slightly outside the ideal 6-month news freshness window relative to this July 2026 research date — still the most current on-record executive framing of Google's rationale as of this pass; flagged per instructions.

The 90-plus/100x power-generation-capacity comparison between Starcloud-1 and Starcloud-2 is a company claim (via GeekWire/TechCrunch) not yet independently verified against Starcloud-2 flight telemetry, since the launch had not yet occurred as of this research date (2026-07-16).
